name: Pubertal growth spurt timing

lead:
The pubertal growth spurt is the period in adolescence when height increases fastest, driven by sex hormones and growth hormone/IGF-1. Most of the height a person will have as an adult is added in this window, so its timing matters for anyone who wants to be taller: it tells you whether growth is likely still to come or has finished.
Girls generally start the spurt earlier than boys, and boys' spurts start later, are slower to peak and last longer, which accounts for most of the average adult height gap between the sexes. Timing is strongly genetic, with nutrition the main environmental influence. Height-focused forums track signs such as shoe size, voice changes and yearly gains to guess where someone is in the spurt.

paras: In practice people estimate where they are in the spurt by tracking measured height over months, noting pubertal signs (body hair, voice change, genital development in boys; breast development and menarche in girls), comparing with parents' heights and growth charts, and sometimes asking a doctor for a bone-age X-ray of the hand and wrist. Looksmaxxing communities also discuss sleep, protein and calorie intake and sport as things that support growth during the window, and ask whether a second spurt might still arrive.

Rapid growth can bring growing pains, temporary clumsiness, and in some adolescents back problems such as adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, which tends to progress around the spurt. Delayed puberty is usually constitutional but can have medical causes, and clinicians evaluate it. Growth-hormone or other hormonal products used to chase extra height carry medical risks and are prescribed only for diagnosed conditions.

angle.text: Adult height is largely decided in this window, so knowing where one is in the spurt tells people how much growth may remain. Sleep, nutrition and general health are discussed as supporting growth during it, while timing itself is mostly set by genetics.

lead: The pubertal growth spurt is the stretch of adolescence in which a young person's height increases faster than at any time since infancy. It is the main period in which final adult height is built, so timing questions (when it starts, when it peaks, when it ends) are central to how people think about height.

Puberty generally begins around 10 to 11 years in girls and 11 to 12 in boys, and the spurt begins in the first half of it; in girls it comes after breast development and before the first period, while in boys it starts later, accelerates more slowly and continues longer before the growth plates fuse [1]. Males are on average about 2 cm shorter than females before puberty but about 13 cm taller as adults, a difference attributed mostly to the later and longer male spurt [1]. Estradiol drives the spurt and growth-plate closure in both sexes, and IGF-1 rising with growth hormone is thought to be a major mediator [1].

In looksmaxxing and height forums, the spurt is the subject of constant questions: whether it has begun, whether one is nearly finished, and whether another could still occur. Clinicians and sports scientists study the same timing through measures such as age at peak height velocity and skeletal age [2].
infobox: Roughly 8-10 cm per year, higher in boys [4]
Height velocity, bone age, age at peak height velocity [2]

paras: Growth in height proceeds fastest in infancy, slows through childhood and then accelerates again during puberty [3]. During the adolescent spurt, height velocity can reach about 8 to 12 cm per year, with peaks of around 9.5 cm per year in boys and 8.3 cm per year in girls reported in one overview [4]. Appetite often increases, and limbs may grow before the trunk, producing a temporary change in proportions [4].

The spurt is usually described by its onset, its peak height velocity (PHV), and the age at which growth stops. In girls the average age of maximal adult height is around 15, in boys around 18 [1]. Boys typically peak around 13 to 14 and girls around 11 to 12 [3].

Genetics account for at least 46% of variation in pubertal timing in well-nourished populations, with nutrition the strongest environmental influence [1]. Twin studies put the heritability of adult height itself at roughly 60 to 80% [3]. Severe malnutrition and neglect have the greatest effect during the critical growth periods [3]. Studies of stunted children in Bangladesh have examined how early-life stunting relates to later pubertal development [5].

Population averages also differ. One overview reports that children of Asian descent may reach skeletal maturity later than those of European descent, and that timing varies by ethnicity [4]. Because individuals vary widely, researchers and clinicians use several markers to estimate maturity, including skeletal age, secondary sex characteristics and anthropometric prediction of age at PHV [2].

Delayed puberty is defined as no breast development by about 13.4 years in girls and no testicular enlargement by 14 years in boys; the most common cause is constitutional delay of growth and puberty, which is a variant of normal timing, while chronic illness or hormonal disorders account for others [6]. Clinicians assess history, growth records and pubertal staging, and boys may be offered treatment [6].

Randomised work on growth hormone therapy has looked at its effects on spontaneous sexual development in children treated for short stature [7]. Such treatment is a medical matter for diagnosed conditions.

Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis typically presents between about age 10 and the end of the growth spurt, and clinicians monitor curves during this period [8]. Idiopathic condylar resorption, a jaw-joint condition, predominantly affects young women around the pubertal spurt [9]. Orthodontists also use growth-spurt stage and cervical vertebral maturation to time treatments such as palatal expansion [10].

On looksmax.org, threads regularly ask whether a spurt has begun, how to tell if one is imminent and when the last spurt happened; titles include questions about a spurt not yet starting and about getting another one [11][12][13]. Posters in these threads commonly cite parents' heights, shoe size, voice changes and past yearly gains. Some ask whether growth-hormone secretagogues such as MK-677 could produce a spurt [14]. Another thread describes a large late increase in height as a personal story [15].

Human research on growth-spurt timing includes longitudinal growth standards for height, height velocity and pubertal stages, a landmark 1976 dataset that is still widely cited [16]. Studies of youth athletes evaluate methods for estimating maturity status and age at PHV, and note that selection into sport follows a maturity-related gradient [2][17]. A randomised trial of calcium supplementation in adolescent girls examined iron status and age at menarche [18]. A registered study (NCT03363802) assesses the pubertal growth spurt in girls using finger bone and molar development [19].
